text: Fusion for Energy (F4E) is the European Union organisation that coordinates the European contribution to the construction of the IFMIF-DONES facility in Granada, Spain, on behalf of Euratom.
The continuous liquid target loop uses liquid lithium to generate the high neutron flux; lithium flows as a free jet across the beam footprint.
The liquid lithium jet is designed to flow at approximately 15 m/s at the beam interaction zone to ensure adequate heat removal and target stability.
The deuteron beam strikes the flowing lithium target with a rectangular footprint of about 200 mm by 50 mm.
The IFMIF-DONES accelerator is designed for a nominal deuteron beam energy of 40 MeV at a beam current of 125 mA.
The Radio Frequency Quadrupole (RFQ) in the injector section operates at a radio frequency of 175 MHz.
The superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) linear accelerator requires a beam current of 125 mA for full-power operation.
The main acceleration cryomodules employ half-wave resonator (HWR) superconducting cavities operating at 175 MHz.
Vacuum pressure in the beamline is maintained at 1e-7 mbar using turbo-molecular pumps and cryogenic pumps.
Beam loss is mitigated by a low-loss lattice, collimators and beam diagnostics to prevent excessive activation of the beam pipe.
The DONES neutron energy spectrum peaks around 14 MeV and is tailored to match the first-wall spectrum of the DEMO fusion reactor for fusion materials testing.
Material samples in the High Flux Test Module (HFTM) are actively cooled by helium gas flowing through channels in the specimen holder.
Boiling of liquid lithium is prevented by maintaining high flow velocity and pressure, keeping lithium subcooled as it absorbs the 5 MW beam power.
Tested reduced-activation steel samples are expected to reach about 20 displacements per atom (dpa) per year in the high-flux region.
The lithium target structural support (backplate) is engineered for an operational cycle of 11 months before dpa-induced embrittlement necessitates component swap.
Impurities such as nitrogen and oxygen are removed from the lithium inventory by cold trapping and gettering with yttrium.
Diagnostics monitoring the liquid lithium free surface include laser-based thickness sensors and videometry for stability.
First-phase testing prioritises Eurofer97 and F82H variants of reduced-activation ferritic/martensitic (RAFM) steels.
Irradiated capsules are transferred from the test module to hot cells via a pneumatic rabbit system and shielded casks for post-irradiation examination.
Safety containment protocols for tritium produced in the lithium loop include double confinement, tritium recovery systems and negative pressure gloveboxes.
IFMIF-DONES is a particle accelerator facility under construction in Granada, Spain, for fusion materials testing.
The DEMO fusion reactor neutron spectrum is widely studied for plasma-facing components and breeding blankets.
Lithium-tritium reactions in the loop are analysed for tritium breeding and inventory control.
The accelerator injector includes an electron cyclotron resonance ion source producing deuterons.
Beam optics in the low-energy beam transport section focus the deuteron beam before the RFQ.
The medium-energy beam transport contains buncher cavities and quadrupole magnets.
Superconducting solenoids provide transverse focusing in the SRF linac cryomodules.
The high-energy beam transport delivers the beam to the lithium target with minimal loss.
Beam diagnostics include beam position monitors, profile monitors and Faraday cups.
The lithium loop includes a heat exchanger to remove the 5 MW deposited by the beam.
Cold traps in the lithium loop collect impurities by condensation at low temperature.
Yttrium getters chemically bind nitrogen and oxygen dissolved in liquid lithium.
The target backplate is made of a RAFM steel to withstand radiation damage.
Post-irradiation examination of samples is performed in hot cells with remote manipulators.
Material samples are encapsulated and placed in the high-flux region of the HFTM.
Neutron flux in DONES reaches about 1e18 n/m2/s in the high-flux test region.
The DEMO reactor requires materials to withstand up to 20 dpa per full-power year.
Eurofer97 is a reduced-activation ferritic-martensitic steel developed for fusion applications.
F82H is a Japanese reduced-activation ferritic-martensitic steel for fusion reactors.
Helium cooling in the HFTM provides efficient heat removal from specimens.
